opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really good question, and honestly it's one we debated a lot internally. The way I think about it is that shipping something as a separate model first is less about the model and more about learning. When you're introducing a genuinely new behavior, like the model being able to schedule things, follow up with you later, and act asynchronously instead of only when you message it, you don't fully know how people will use it until it's in their hands.

If you fold that straight into the core model on day one, a few things happen. First, you risk regressions. The core model is used by hundreds of millions of people for everything, and you don't want a new capability that's still a bit rough to change how it behaves on normal tasks. For example, it might start trying to create reminders when you didn't ask, or get weird about time. Second, it's much harder to get a clean signal. If it's a separate surface, you can see exactly who opts in, what kinds of tasks they set up, where it fails, and what they expected it to do but it didn't.

So the separate release is almost like a research preview. It lets us iterate quickly on the post-training side, things like when the model should proactively suggest a task, how it phrases notifications, and how it handles ambiguity like "remind me next week." We can change it without touching the flagship model's behavior.

Then once we understand the patterns, we can distill those learnings back into the main model, and that's the end state you want. Users shouldn't have to pick a special model to get reminders. It should just be one of the things the assistant naturally knows how to do, alongside search, canvas, and memory. I see it as a progression: prototype the capability in isolation, learn from real usage, and then integrate it so it feels native.

There's also a product philosophy piece. I think the future of these assistants is moving from purely reactive chat toward something more proactive and asynchronous, where the model works on your behalf even when you're not there. Tasks is a pretty small first step toward that, and releasing it on its own let us test that bigger idea in a low-stakes way.

r001.rationale: The response says the end state is to integrate Tasks into the main model so users do not need a separate model for reminders or other features.

r002.rationale: It explains that immediate integration risks regressions and makes it harder to get a clear usage signal, while a separate release can be changed without affecting the flagship model.

r003.rationale: It describes learning from opt-in users’ task usage, failures, and expectations, then distilling those learnings into the main model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this was something we debated a lot internally. The honest answer is that Tasks was a product bet first, and the scheduling capability was something we didn't want to wait on for the next big model cycle to validate.

When you ship something as a separate model in the picker, you're basically creating a sandbox. You can route a very specific set of behaviors to it, you can tune the post-training really narrowly for things like understanding time, understanding recurrence, knowing when to actually fire versus when to ask a clarifying question, and you don't risk regressing the base model on everything else. The core model has to be good at a thousand things, and every time you add a new capability like scheduling, you're trading off against that distribution. Doing it in isolation let us move fast and learn from real usage without that fear.

The other piece is that Tasks is fundamentally about the model acting on your behalf when you're not in the conversation. That's a different trust posture than a chat reply. We wanted to see how people actually used it, what they scheduled, where it broke, how often it did something they didn't intend, before baking that behavior into the default experience for hundreds of millions of people. A separate model gives you a smaller, more opt-in population to learn from.

And then the long-term intent was always to collapse it back in. I think of these separate model releases as scaffolding. You build the behavior, you collect the data and the evals, you figure out what the right defaults are, and then once it's robust, it becomes a native capability the main model just has. Users shouldn't have to pick a model to set a reminder. That's a failure of the interface, not a feature.

So I'd frame it less as "we think this should be a separate model" and more as "this is how you ship a new agentic behavior responsibly before you make it universal."

r001.rationale: The response says Tasks was always intended to be folded into the main model, so users would not need to choose a model for reminders.

r002.rationale: It explains that isolating scheduling behaviors allows focused tuning, faster learning, and avoids risking regressions or tradeoffs in the core model while validating a different trust posture.

r003.rationale: It says the separate release would gather real usage data and evaluations to establish robust behavior and defaults before making Tasks a native capability of the main model.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a way to learn with a more focused product first. With Tasks, you’re moving from a model that responds when you ask it something to a system that can do something for you later. That introduces questions around intent, timing, and how much control the user should have.

Releasing it separately gives you room to understand those interactions and improve the behavior before making it part of the default experience. Longer term, I’d want that to feel seamless. You shouldn’t have to think about which model to choose just to ask ChatGPT to follow up on something tomorrow. But integration should come once the behavior is reliable and the interaction makes sense.

r001.rationale: The response says the long-term goal is a seamless ChatGPT experience where users do not need to choose a model, conveying consolidation into one model.

r002.rationale: It says a separate release creates room to understand interactions and improve behavior, but does not state that operational difficulties make separate release easier than immediate integration.

r003.rationale: The response mentions learning about interactions and improving behavior before integration, but does not clearly identify feedback from the separate release as the basis for that improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as a way to learn about the interaction before we fold it into the core model. With Tasks, you’re moving from a model that responds when you ask it something to one that can do something later and come back to you. That changes what users expect: Can I trust it to follow through? Does it understand when I want something done? How do I change or cancel it?

Releasing it separately gives us a more contained space to understand those questions and improve the experience. Ideally, users shouldn’t have to think about which model supports tasks. They should just be able to express what they want, and the system should know how to handle it. But getting there involves learning what that behavior should look like.

r001.rationale: It says users ideally should not need to think about which model supports Tasks and that the system should handle the request, conveying the goal of bringing the feature into one model.

r002.rationale: It gives learning about user expectations as a reason to release separately, but does not say operational difficulties make immediate integration harder.

r003.rationale: It describes using the separate release as a contained way to learn how the behavior should work and improve the experience before folding Tasks into the core model.
